replacement: From the house of my childhood I have brought away nothing but precious memories. No memories are more precious than those of early childhood in one’s first home, and that is almost always so, as long as there is any love and harmony in the family at all. Even a bad home can leave precious memories, if only the heart knows how to find what is precious in it. Among my memories of home I count my memories of the Bible, which I was very eager to read as a child. I had a book of Scripture history then, with excellent pictures, called _A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament_. I learned to read from it. It lies on my shelf now, and I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I could read, I was moved to devotion for the first time, at eight years old. I remember it well. My mother took me alone to the service on the Monday before Easter. (I do not remember where my brother was.) The day was fine. I remember it today as though I saw it now: the incense rose from the censer and floated softly upwards, and up in the cupola it mingled, in rising waves, with the sunlight streaming through the little window. The sight stirred me, and for the first time in my life I consciously received the seed of God’s word in my heart. A youth came out into the middle of the church carrying a big book. It was so large that I thought he could scarcely carry it. He laid it on the reading desk and opened it and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something that was read in the church of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, who had great wealth: so many camels, so many sheep and asses. His children feasted, and he loved them dearly and prayed for them. “It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.” Then the devil came before the Lord, together with the sons of God, and told the Lord that he had gone up and down the earth and under the earth. “And have you considered my servant Job?” God asked him. God boasted to the devil of His great and holy servant, and the devil laughed at God’s words. “Give him over to me, and You will see that Your servant will murmur against You and curse Your name.” So God gave up the just man He loved so much into the devil’s hands. And the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all at once, like a thunderbolt from heaven. Job tore his mantle and fell to the ground and cried aloud, “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever and ever.”
